transcript:
Header: 2026-01-15 16:00 UTC — Duration ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rajat Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Park (Redwood CSM), Liam O'Connor (CISO, Zenova), Priya Rao (SRE Lead), Daniel Vega (Cloud Architect), Ana Morales (Legal)

--- Optional auto-summary (auto): quick note: we'll cover SSO, KMS, logs, incident runbook and SLA tiers then agree next steps.

[00:00:00] Maya: All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, um, we wanted to run through the tabletop for incident response and how that maps to our Private and Dedicated offerings, and specifically your data residency and KMS needs.
[00:00:18] Liam: Thanks Maya. Uh we gave some context in the pre-read, but main ask is we need to make sure a Redwood deployment meets PCI scope and our bank audits, so like, RTO is 60 minutes for critical flow and RPO is 15 minutes ideally.
[00:00:34] Rajat: Got it, yeah we noted the RTO/RPO. Quick callout — those numbers are aggressive, but from a deployment standpoint doable with Dedicated pools + cross-region failover and KV cache warming. We'll talk through tradeoffs.
[00:00:52] Priya: Can I interrupt — when you say "KV cache warming" do you mean the key value cache? our concern is warm start time for stateful sessions.
[00:01:01] Rajat: Yeah sorry transcription: KV cache, yes. The runtime supports prefix caching and checkpoint snapshots so burst failover is faster. But you do need some replication.
[00:01:14] Daniel: For our environment we need keys to stay in EMEA region only — so KMS keys must be regionally resident. Do you support customer-managed keys in an HSM?
[00:01:25] Maya: Yes, we support Bring-Your-Own-KMS for Private and Dedicated. For Private (VPC/on-prem) you can plug in your KMS or HSM. There's an integration pattern we can share. For hosted it's Redwood-managed keys but with encryption at rest and in-transit.
[00:01:41] Ana: Legal question — auditability: we need unmodified audit logs retained for 7 years and proof of immutability for audits. Is that supported?
[00:01:49] Elena: Real quick, we typically retain per-customer audit logs for configurable retention windows; for Private we can configure offsite WORM storage and integrate with your SIEM. For hosted there are stricter limits but enterprise add-ons exist.
[00:02:05] Liam: When you say WORM, is that an object store policy or do you use an append-only log with signatures? Auditors usually prefer signed, append-only chains.
[00:02:14] Rajat: We can provide immutable storage options — the on-prem pattern uses an append-only collector with signed entries and SHA checks. For cloud we can export to your S3 bucket with object lock enabled. We'll attach the doc.
[00:02:29] Priya: Ok. I'd like to do a quick tabletop. Scenario: primary region goes down — we need to fail to secondary within RTO=60m. Walk us through steps and who we call.
[00:02:40] Maya: Sure. Step one: automated detection triggers alert via monitoring -> Redwood alerting to SRE + customer contacts if configured. Step two: automated routing moves traffic to secondary region/model variant. Step three: cache warm/rehydration. Step four: manual DR runbook if auto-failover doesn't reach SLO.
[00:02:58] Daniel: Who is on the escalation ladder from Redwood? We need names, phone numbers, and SLAs for response times.
[00:03:05] Maya: We'll provide a runbook with on-call roster: SE-level response within 15 minutes for P1 on Dedicated/Private customers with SLA, and engineering escalation within 60 minutes. That's part of the enterprise SLA pack.
[00:03:17] Liam: Is that 15 minutes to acknowledge or to start remediation? auditors ask for time-to-ack.
[00:03:23] Rajat: Acknowledge within 15, initial triage/action within 60 for P1. We'll add that phrasing to the runbook.
[00:03:30] Priya: What about the data plane — if we switch regions, is there a risk of landing in non-resident region? We can't have tokens or logs cross under any circumstances.
[00:03:41] Maya: For Private and Dedicated we can lock routing policies to region sets. Automated fallback to a different region only occurs if you enable cross-region failover. If you require strict residency, we recommend Dedicated with same-region failover or a cold DR procedure.
[00:03:55] Daniel: For Zenova we need keys in EU-West-1 only and logs to stay in EU. If the primary goes down, we need a manual DR failover to the EU secondary; auto-failover is not permitted.
[00:04:07] Maya: Noted — that adds a manual step to the runbook; we can implement a gated failover where the customer initiates 'promote' once they verify.
[00:04:15] Priya: Great. Next: SSO. We use Okta with SCIM for provisioning and SAML for SSO. Role mapping needs to map Okta groups to RBAC within Redwood. How granular is that?
[00:04:27] Rajat: We support SAML 2.0, SCIM provisioning for users and groups. RBAC can be mapped to group attributes; you can have fine-grained roles like "ops-write" vs "ops-read". There are some limits on object-level permissions today, but group-level roles are fully supported.
[00:04:45] Liam: Is there support for session timeouts and forced re-auth? Auditors want session expiry enforcement.
[00:04:51] Elena: You can configure session durations via SAML assertion settings and we also support session revocation via SCIM. For Private deploys you get additional session policies.
[00:05:01] Ana: Do you keep login events in the same audit logs for compliance? We want to show chain-of-custody.
[00:05:07] Rajat: Yes auth events and API token use are logged. We include user id, source IP, action, and token fingerprint. We can also stream to your SIEM with a schema.
[00:05:17] Priya: On tokens — do you support short-lived tokens only? We prefer ephemeral tokens with automatic rotation.
[00:05:22] Maya: For hosted we have API keys with TTL options and support for rotating keys. For Private you can enforce short-lived session tokens integrated with your identity provider.
[00:05:31] [00:05:31] Speaker 1: (mumble) the pre-read mentioned encryption in transit standards?
[00:05:36] Rajat: TLS 1.3 by default in all flows; internal service-to-service comms are mTLS within the cluster for Private.
[00:05:43] Priya: Ok. Back to incident steps: who declares an incident inside Redwood? Is there a P1/P2 taxonomy?
[00:05:50] Maya: Yes, we have a P0/P1/P2 taxonomy. P1 = critical production impacting. Declaration can be automatic (monitoring) or by customer request. Once declared, Redwood opens an incident channel, posts updates every 15 minutes, and assigns an incident commander.
[00:06:05] Daniel: We need the incident postmortem template ahead of time so our audit team knows what to expect.
[00:06:09] Maya: We'll share the postmortem template and an example from a redacted incident.
[00:06:12] Priya: Are runbooks editable by our SRE so we can annotate steps?
[00:06:16] Elena: For Private customers you get a customer-managed runbook repo; for Dedicated we can provide a shared editable page.
[00:06:22] Liam: Let's talk SLA credits — if you miss the uptime, what's the credit window and how is it calculated?
[00:06:29] Rajat: Credits are pro-rated monthly based on affected region and service layer. For Dedicated we offer uptime tiers with financial credits; we'll send the SLA doc.
[00:06:37] Ana: One more legal item — if we take emergency access during incident triage, how is that gated and audited?
[00:06:43] Maya: Emergency access is role-based, time-limited, and is recorded in the audit log. We require a customer approval flow for privileged actions unless you give a standing emergency exception.
[00:06:54] Daniel: Do you have a dead-man switch? like if Redwood can't respond we want an automated unlock or to assume control to restore service.
[00:07:02] Rajat: We don't do unilateral customer takeovers. The typical pattern is a lockbox key so you can bring up a customer-managed fallback or run an exported runtime image in your environment. For Private installs you can of course self-host.
[00:07:17] Priya: Could you walk us through a sample timeline for an RPO breach where a storage layer failed and we lost the last 30 minutes of logs?
[00:07:26] Maya: Sure: T0 detection, notify customer, attempt recovery from replication, if failed then invoke point-in-time restore from backups — restore time depends on data size — estimated 30-90 minutes in typical configs. If that exceeds RTO we'll engage manual DR and escalate to engineering to do restore from snapshots.
[00:07:45] Liam: So we need guarantees around backup cadence — how frequently do you snapshot token caches and persistent state?
[00:07:52] Rajat: For Dedicated we recommend snapshot cadence aligned to your RPO; we can do incremental every 5–15 minutes for critical metadata and hourly full snapshots. We'll propose a snapshot plan in the spike.
[00:08:05] Daniel: About the private-deploy spike: we want Redwood SE to run a one-day deploy in our lab with KMS integration and for you to restore a simulated P1 failure. Can you do that in two weeks?
[00:08:16] Rajat: Yes, we can run a 4–8 hour hands-on spike plus a follow-up 2–4 hour restore run. We just need an infra contact and temporary creds.
[00:08:25] Maya: We'll include a checklist of what we need.
[00:08:28] Ana: On compliance, SOC 2 Type II coverage — do you have a current report and is the scope covering dedicated instances?
[00:08:34] Elena: We have SOC2 Type II for our control plane and hosted service. For Dedicated/Private, the control scope depends on configuration; we'll provide the mapping document so auditors can see which controls are in customer scope.
[00:08:47] Liam: And ISO 27001?
[00:08:49] Maya: We maintain ISO attestation for the platform — again Private deploys may change scope but we have a compliance pack.
[00:08:55] Priya: Ok I'd like to drill on audit log schema: is the log tamper evidence signed per entry?
[00:09:01] Rajat: For the append-only collector we add per-entry signing metadata. The export has both signed entries and an index for quick search.
[00:09:11] Daniel: For our auditors we also need a chain-of-custody diagram for keys and for backups — who signs off, how keys are rotated.
[00:09:20] Maya: We'll include a key lifecycle diagram and rotation policy. We support KMS rotation schedules and manual key destruction only under controlled flows.
[00:09:30] Liam: Let's capture the sprint: we want a short document mapping our regulatory needs to the recommended Redwood config and a runbook we can reference in audits.
[00:09:38] Maya: That's on us — we'll produce a tailored 'Zenova compliance map' plus the runbook template.
[00:09:44] [00:09:44] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)
[00:09:46] Priya: Quick question on telemetry — if you stream metrics and traces to our observability stack, is there a chance sensitive payload leaks in traces?
[00:09:54] Rajat: We redact PII at the SDK layer before traces are emitted; by default we don't capture user prompt text in traces. If you want full trace capture that's opt-in with special handling.
[00:10:06] Daniel: How do you handle legal holds? if audit requires retaining a subset of data beyond retention window.
[00:10:12] Elena: We can set retention overrides and legal-hold flags on exports; that's supported for Dedicated and Private customers.
[00:10:18] Ana: Ok for contract language: we need an addendum for emergency access, key management responsibilities, and a 7-year log retention guarantee. Will Redwood accept that contract language?
[00:10:27] Maya: We'll need legal review. We'll flag any points that are commercially sensitive, but typically we handle KMS responsibility split and retention addenda as enterprise add-ons.
[00:10:36] Liam: One last scenario — ransomware impacting storage in primary region where backups may be encrypted by the attacker. How do you prevent that?
[00:10:45] Rajat: Defense-in-depth: immutable backups, WORM for audit logs, MFA on backup vault, and separation of duties for key admins. For Private you can maintain air-gapped backups.
[00:10:57] Priya: So next steps recap?
[00:11:00] Maya: Sure: (1) Maya to share SOC2/ISO pack + compliance map by 2026-01-18. (2) Rajat to schedule private-deploy feasibility spike by 2026-01-22. (3) Daniel to send RTO/RPO and DR contact list by 2026-01-20. (4) Redwood legal to review retention addendum and respond.
[00:11:20] Daniel: We'll expect the runbook and sample postmortem.
[00:11:23] Maya: We'll attach a pointer to the runbook template in the follow-up email and include links to our KMS integration notes and audit log schema.
[00:11:31] Liam: Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[00:11:34] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

--- Transcript end. Notes: minor transcription errors present (e.g., KV/"KV cash", occasional speaker mislabels). Shared artifacts referenced: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2-pack (placeholder), runbook template (link in follow-up)."
